title: Convertible scarf-cowl
subtitle: A scarf with a button loop that converts into a cowl.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in 2x2 rib on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide by 160 cm long, with a large button and a button loop at one end so the two ends can be fastened together to wear as a cowl. The rib fabric is reversible so both scarf mode and cowl mode look neat on both sides.
sourceNotes: Convertible scarf-cowl accessories derive from Victorian infinity scarf and comforter patterns in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. The button-and-loop fastening is a modern addition.
heroPrompt: A finished convertible scarf-cowl in warm amber aran-weight yarn shown in two positions: one showing the scarf hanging straight, one showing it fastened with a button into a cowl loop.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small yarn-over buttonhole worked at the end of a row that creates an opening large enough to pass a button through. Used here to convert the scarf into a cowl when fastened.
A rib pattern alternating two knit stitches with two purl stitches on every row, giving a stretchy, reversible fabric.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat in
2x2 rib
on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide and 160 cm long. One end has a
button loop
worked into the bind-off row. A large wooden or horn button is sewn to the other end. Fastening the button creates a cowl; unfastening it gives a straight scarf.

Flat construction was chosen because the convertible function requires a length that can be worn either wrapped or fastened into a loop, and flat knitting gives the cleanest finished edges for a button fastening. The 2x2 rib is reversible so both modes of wear look identical on both sides. The finished scarf needs about 380 m (approximately 220 g) of aran-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any aran-weight yarn. Wool gives the best elasticity for rib.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer

items.name: Large button, 30 to 40 mm diameter
items.substitutions: A horn, wood, or large leather button suits the rib aesthetic.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. In 2x2 rib relaxed the gauge is approximately 14 sts per 10 cm. Swatch at least 6 cm in pattern, measure unstretched. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.4 cm at this stitch count. Row gauge drift across the full 352 rows changes the finished length by up to 14 cm, which significantly affects how the cowl mode sits.
Stitches used

K (knit), P (purl), 2x2 rib: [K2, P2] across. YO (yarn over): bring yarn over the needle tip to create a new stitch (used in the button loop). K2tog: knit two stitches together to close the button loop.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 36 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is a multiple of 4 for 2x2 rib. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 36 stitches: (15.7 x 36) / 10 + 15 = 56.5 + 15 = about 72 cm. Leave at least 72 cm of tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Body
Row 1 (RS): *K2, P2; repeat from * to end. (36 sts)
Row 2 (WS): *P2, K2; repeat from * to end. (36 sts)
Repeat rows 1 and 2 until the scarf measures 160 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately row 176 of 352 body rows), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 176 you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Button loop bind-off

On the final right-side row, work the button loop when you reach the centre of the row: K2, P2, K2, P2, K2, P2, *YO, K2tog* (this creates the button loop hole), then continue in rib to end. Work the standard bind-off on the wrong-side row that follows, binding off in pattern (P the P stitches, K the K stitches).
Check the button fits through the YO, K2tog loop before finishing. If the button is too large for the loop, work a second YO, K2tog adjacent to the first to create a larger opening.
Button attachment

Sew the button to the cast-on end of the scarf, centred on the width. Use a doubled length of the same yarn or a strong sewing thread in a matching colour. Position the button on the right side of the fabric at approximately 3 cm from the cast-on edge so the button loop sits flat when fastened.
Common faults
Button loop too small for the chosen button. Always test the loop size against the button before binding off. The YO, K2tog loop stretches slightly in rib but not as much as the body fabric.

Rib alignment shifting after the button loop row. The YO, K2tog replaces two stitches without changing the count, but the stitches land in a different part of the rib pattern at that point. Work the following bind-off row in pattern across the whole row, not just around the loop.

Scarf too short to fasten as a cowl with comfortable ease. The 160 cm length fastened into a loop gives approximately 80 cm circumference, which is worn with a single generous loop around the neck. If you prefer a tighter loop, reduce the length by 10 to 15 cm.
Finishing
Weave in both tails at each end and trim. Sew the button to the cast-on end. Steam the rib gently to relax the fabric if it has grown in width.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Do not machine wash if the button is a natural material such as horn, wood, or shell. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next
The infinity cowl removes the button entirely by seaming the two ends together permanently. The ribbed cowl works the same rib pattern as a seamless in-the-round tube from the beginning.
